summary: Points out a security flaw in widely deployed resolvers: the way they add search suffixes to partial domain names can be exploited. The memo describes the flaw, a real case, and a fix.

plainLanguage.summary: A resolver may complete a partial domain name by adding endings from a search list. This memo explains how an unsafe list can send users to an unintended host and recommends keeping the search within local control.

questions: dns resolver search list security problem
what is the dns search list vulnerability
why do resolvers limit search lists
what is a rooted domain name
why should resolver searches stay local
subtitle: Why resolver search lists for partial names must stay within local control.

tldr.problem: Some resolvers add search-domain suffixes to partial names, which can make a lookup reach an unintended host outside local control.
tldr.mechanism: The memo says resolvers must limit search lists to locally administered parts of the domain name space and try dotted names as rooted names first.
tldr.outcome: BIND 4.9.2 narrows its implicit search list; additional search alternatives must be configured explicitly. This RFC is Informational.

today: RFC 1535 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How Search Lists Complete Names
sections.content:
Domain Name System (DNS) resolvers translate names into addresses and other resource records. A fully qualified domain name can be written with a final dot; a name without that dot is not rooted. Some resolvers based on BSD BIND try partial names by adding domains from a search list until they find a record.

The RFC's example has a user at Machine.Tech.ACES.COM trying UnivHost.University.EDU. The resolver may append Tech.ACES.COM, then ACES.COM, then COM, before trying the name as rooted.
sections.plainLanguage: When a name is incomplete, a resolver may try it with several endings. A match on an unintended ending can send the user somewhere else.

sections.title: How the Search Can Be Intercepted
sections.content:
The memo describes a case involving the EDU.COM domain and a wildcard CNAME record. The record could cause connections from .COM sites to .EDU sites to end at one machine in the private edu.com subdomain.

A specific name, such as harvard.edu.com, could also point to a target host that presents a Harvard.edu login banner. The underlying issue is that a resolver may search beyond the locally administered part of a name and into publicly administered names.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker could register a name that a resolver tries while completing a partial name. The user might then connect to a host pretending to be the intended one.

sections.title: Boundaries for Resolver Searches
sections.content:
At a minimum, a resolver must respect the boundary between local and public name administration. Its search list should stop at the part of the domain name space controlled by the local administrator. This lets local users try progressively less specific names without searching beyond that boundary.

The memo says resolvers should not use implicit search lists beyond the host's immediate parent domain. If they use implicit lists, they must limit them to locally administered subdomains, and they should not ship with explicit lists that repeat the problem. A name containing a dot should be treated as fully qualified and tried as rooted first. BIND 4.9.2 narrows implicit searches to the first and last candidates; extra alternatives need explicit configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolvers should try the complete name first when it contains a dot. Any added endings must stay inside the part of the name space managed locally.
